source.title: DeepFleet: Multi-Agent Foundation Models for Mobile Robots
source.authors: Ameya Agaskar; S. Siva; William Pickering; Kyle O'Brien; Charles Kekeh; Ang Li; Brianna Gallo Sarker; A. Chua; Mayur Nemade; Charun Thattai; Jiaming Di; Isaac Iyengar; Ramya Dharoor; Dino Kirouani; J. Erskine; T. Hegazy; S. Niekum; Usman A. Khan; Federico Pecora; Joseph W. Durham

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The arXiv header identifies version v3; no apparent truncation or garbling affects the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs scaling experiments on robot-fleet forecasting models, extending scaling-law questions to a different training regime and domain. It reports loss curves and compute-optimal model/data scaling.
record.gate_note: The scaling experiments in Figures 3–6 bear on V5. The text also cites language-model scaling studies, but cited results are not this study’s findings. Table 2 compares four architectures at different sizes and data amounts, so it does not isolate architecture effects at a fixed parameter count; that comparison is not recorded as a result for V4. Downstream applications are described as future aims, not evaluated results.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own Chinchilla-style scaling experiments on a new domain: robot-fleet action and state forecasting pretrained on warehouse movement data. It reports loss against data, parameters and FLOPs, isoFLOP curves, and a power-law fit of compute-optimal model and data size. These results bear on V5, whether the power-law form holds beyond text pretraining. There are no language-model experiments, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling model size, compute and data improves performance for RC and GF. For GF they derive compute-optimal model/data power laws, fitted over about two orders of magnitude and extrapolated to 10^22 FLOPs (about 1B parameters, 6.6M episodes). RC needs longer training before a quantitative scaling law can be fitted. All scaling evidence is training loss, and the extrapolation is not tested.
record.recipe_differences: This is a robot-fleet forecasting study, not a language-model scaling-law reproduction. It studies training loss and compute-optimal model size and floor-episode count in RC and GF models.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes what scaling evidence is available: GF provides a clear loss envelope and fit-able isoFLOP curves, while RC requires longer training for complete isoFLOP curves.
record.problems: The scaling study is limited to RC and GF; RC curves are explicitly incomplete. The plotted loss curves have no reported numerical values or fitted loss exponents in the text. The compute-optimal power-law result is reported for only two orders of magnitude and includes an extrapolation. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible scaling results were left out. Table 2's cross-architecture performance comparison is not an isolated scaling result or a fixed-parameter-count architecture test, so it is not included as a row.

untested.parts: All of it: no language-model pretraining loss scaling.
All of it for language models. Within this study, the GF extrapolation to 10^22 FLOPs is proposed but never checked against an actual large run.
The language-model parameter/token split. An analogous compute-optimal fit exists for GF robot models, but no exponents are reported, so it cannot be compared with Kaplan or Hoffmann.
All of it. Table 2 compares architectures at different sizes and data amounts, not shape at a fixed parameter count.

Only robot-fleet forecasting is tested; images, video, repeated data and fine-tuning are not. The loss is training loss only. No power-law fit or exponent is reported for loss against data, parameters or compute.
All of it: Table 2's downstream-like metrics (DTW, CDE) are not related to scale.

record.verdict_notes: Domain: multi-agent robot-fleet behaviour-cloning and forecasting, not text. The related-work section claims scaling laws 'over several orders of magnitude', but the actual fit spans about two. No exponents, held-out losses or uncertainties are reported. R3/R4 duplicate R1/R2 because Figure 3 plots loss against data only, with model size as a series. R1–R4 show only the direction of improvement, so they carry no verdict label. Table 2 is correctly excluded: it is not a scaling result.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling for language models with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs.
The language-model parameter/token compute-optimal split, including whether parameter and token counts grow equally or at different rates.
Architecture effects on loss at a fixed parameter count.

Tests robot-fleet forecasting only. It does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other modalities and training regimes. Its loss curves are shown in figures, but the paper does not report fitted loss power laws for loss against parameters, data, or compute.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss; downstream applications are proposed but not evaluated.
Whether setup or fitting choices change the exponents or cause curves to bend away from power laws.
